strongest_objection: The map's whole warrant is 'the arithmetic in one illustrative case', and the arithmetic is wrong or the stated mechanism false in the places an operator would check first. Ten votes a share gives eight percent of the economics fifty-five percent of the vote, but at ten votes a share eight percent carries forty-six and a half percent; fifty-five needs about eleven. Ninety-day guillotine and the edge built on it say lapsed options return pro rata to the holders who stayed, but lapsed options return to the pool, which the board regrants, so nothing lands pro rata on anyone. Warrant on the loan explains the warrant's absence from the cap table by its being worth nothing on the day it is struck, which is not a mechanism; an at-the-money warrant has option value and most fully diluted tables carry it. Stack that eats the common calls a sixty-million exit on fifty raised a six-fold win with no number in the case that is six times anything. And Carve-out at the door picks the one exit price at which the carve-out drains the common nothing: against a hundred and twenty of preference the common gets zero with or without it, so the carrier only bites in the band just under the stack's top, which the item should say. None of this touches the item type, the itinerary, or the edges' shapes; the strange members are real and survive. I tried to collapse Cap as option into Ratchet after the fact, which the author's own note calls the same put written twice, and could not: the cap is a single-shot put with a strike fixed before any price exists, extinguished at conversion, and the ratchet is a standing put that survives every round.

items.item: Below the threshold: grants each too small to be argued over, an advisor's quarter point, a consultant's half, a friend's tenth, are approved without the process a large grant gets and sum above the threshold the process exists for; agreed over coffee, understood by nobody as a total; six advisors at a half point each, vesting monthly with no cliff, is three percent, more than the Series A lead's board observer got for a check; not the size of any grant but the granularity that keeps each one below attention, and the tell is that nobody in the room can name the sum.
items.why: Mechanism is sound (granularity under the attention threshold), but the comparison 'more than the Series A lead's board observer got for a check' is garbled: an observer is a person, not a holder, and no reader can reconstruct what got compared to what.
items.repair: Below the threshold: grants each too small to be argued over, an advisor's quarter point, a consultant's half, a friend's tenth, are approved without the process a large grant gets and sum above the threshold the process exists for; agreed over coffee, understood by nobody as a total; six advisors at a half point each, vesting monthly with no cliff, is three percent, a seed check's slice with no check behind it; not the size of any grant but the granularity that keeps each one below attention, and the tell is that nobody in the room can name the sum.

items.item: Warrant on the loan: venture debt carries warrant coverage, a fraction of the principal in warrants struck at the last round's price, so a lender who bore no equity risk holds equity if the company rises; agreed in the loan agreement and never entered on the cap table because the warrants are worth nothing the day they are struck; three million borrowed with ten-percent coverage at a ten-million post is three hundred thousand of shares at last-round price, three percent of the company on a loan that also charges twelve; not interest, which is paid in cash and ends, but a share count fixed at signing whose value waits on the exit, and the tell is a cap table that omits the debt file.
items.why: The reason given for the warrant's invisibility, 'never entered on the cap table because the warrants are worth nothing the day they are struck', is a false mechanism: an at-the-money warrant has option value, and fully diluted tables routinely carry warrants. What hides it is the document it lives in, which the seriation note already says. 'Bore no equity risk' also overstates; the lender bears credit risk.
items.repair: Warrant on the loan: venture debt carries warrant coverage, a fraction of the principal in warrants struck at the last round's price, so a lender who bore credit risk and no equity risk holds equity if the company rises; agreed in the loan agreement and carried in the debt file rather than the round documents, so it is priced at zero in every conversation that is not about the exit and missing from the cap table the founder quotes from memory; three million borrowed with ten-percent coverage at a ten-million post is three hundred thousand of shares at last-round price, three percent of the company on a loan that also charges twelve; not interest, which is paid in cash and ends, but a share count fixed at signing whose value waits on the exit, and the tell is a cap table that omits the debt file.

items.item: Cap as option: a valuation cap is a ceiling, not a price, so the SAFE converts at the lower of the cap and the discounted round price, and the holder is long an option whose value grows with the uncertainty of the next round; agreed when the founder treats the cap as the valuation she raised at, understood by the investor as a floor on his percentage; a SAFE at a ten million cap converts at ten if the A prices at twenty and at six if the A prices at six, so the 'ten million round' was a ten-or-less round; not a discount, which is a fixed ratio, but a payoff bent at the cap, and the tell is a founder quoting the cap as her last valuation.
items.why: Tested as the left neighbor against Ratchet after the fact; separates (see neighbor_test). The arithmetic (converts at ten if the A prices at twenty, at six if at six) is right for a cap without a discount, and the item says 'lower of the cap and the discounted round price', which covers the discount case.

items.item: Ratchet after the fact: anti-dilution resets an earlier round's conversion price when a later round prices lower, so the earlier investor receives shares as if she had bought at the lower price and the common pays for them; agreed in a clause the founder skips because she does not intend a down round, understood by the investor as the term that makes a high price safe; under a full ratchet a Series A that bought a quarter at four dollars sees a B at two and doubles its share count before the B buys a share, and broad-based weighted average softens this by the B's size; observed in Square's 2015 offering, where a Series E floor of $18.56 against a nine-dollar offer issued the E about ten million extra shares, as reported; not a repricing, which the investor did not buy, but a repricing in one direction only, so the earlier money holds a put on the later price.
items.why: Tested as the right neighbor against Cap as option; separates. Full-ratchet arithmetic is right (a quarter at four, B at two, share count doubles). The Square 2015 figures, a $18.56 floor against a nine-dollar offer and about ten million extra Series E shares, match what was reported and are marked as reported.

items.item: Reset with the trigger in the other hand: the Series A puts a founder's already-vested shares back on a schedule with a repurchase right at cost, so a founder three years in and three-quarters vested is a quarter vested again; agreed under the sentence 'we need you committed' and understood by both sides as a commitment device, but the board that can end her employment is, after the round, a board the investor sits on, and forfeited shares are retired, which lifts every remaining holder pro rata including the one who voted; a founder with thirty percent removed twelve months after the reset keeps under half of her shares, and the seventeen percent of the company that returns is spread over whoever remains; not vesting, which any hire accepts, but a forfeiture whose trigger and beneficiary are the same hand.
items.why: The mechanism sentence is careful, 'a board the investor sits on', and the arithmetic is exact (a quarter vested plus twelve months of four years is 43.75 percent kept, and 30 times 56.25 is the seventeen percent returned). The discriminator then promotes sitting on the board to holding the trigger: 'trigger and beneficiary are the same hand'. At a Series A the investor is one seat and one pro rata beneficiary among all remaining holders. Keep the strangeness, state it at its true strength.
items.repair: Reset with the trigger in the other hand: the Series A puts a founder's already-vested shares back on a schedule with a repurchase right at cost, so a founder three years in and three-quarters vested is a quarter vested again; agreed under the sentence 'we need you committed' and understood by both sides as a commitment device, but the board that can end her employment is, after the round, a board the investor sits on, and forfeited shares are retired, which lifts every remaining holder pro rata including the one who voted; a founder with thirty percent removed twelve months after the reset keeps under half of her shares, and the seventeen percent of the company that returns is spread over whoever remains; not vesting, which any hire accepts, but a forfeiture whose trigger sits with a board on which its beneficiaries vote.

items.item: Ninety-day guillotine: vested options must be exercised within ninety days of leaving, paying the strike and the tax on the spread, or they lapse back to the pool, so the carrier of an employee's ownership back to the company is a purchase price on the exit door, due on the day she can least afford it; agreed in the plan document every hire signs unread, written by counsel under a tax rule; fifty thousand vested options at a two-dollar strike against a twenty-dollar appraisal is a hundred thousand in cash and a nine-hundred-thousand spread the tax bill can treat as income, so a departing engineer with a mortgage forfeits ownership she spent four years earning; not a vesting term, since the shares had vested, but a toll on keeping them, and what lapses returns pro rata to the holders who stayed.
items.why: The mechanism sentence says the options 'lapse back to the pool'; the discriminator then says 'what lapses returns pro rata to the holders who stayed'. Those are different destinations and only the first is true: lapsed options are unallocated pool, counted on the fully diluted table as before and regranted by the board, so nothing lands pro rata on anyone. The pro rata claim belongs to the reset (retired shares) and was carried over by analogy.
items.repair: Ninety-day guillotine: vested options must be exercised within ninety days of leaving, paying the strike and the tax on the spread, or they lapse back to the pool, so the carrier of an employee's ownership back to the company is a purchase price on the exit door, due on the day she can least afford it; agreed in the plan document every hire signs unread, written by counsel under a tax rule; fifty thousand vested options at a two-dollar strike against a twenty-dollar appraisal is a hundred thousand in cash and a nine-hundred-thousand spread the tax bill can treat as income, so a departing engineer with a mortgage forfeits ownership she spent four years earning; not a vesting term, since the shares had vested, but a toll on keeping them, and what lapses returns to a pool the same board regrants, so the beneficiary is whoever is hired next and the founder whose next refill is smaller.

items.item: Stack that eats the common: each round's preferred takes its money back before common sees anything, so the founder's percentage is a share of the exit only above the price at which conversion beats preference, and below it a good price pays the common almost nothing; agreed round by round as 'one times non-participating, standard', understood by every investor as the whole point and read by the founder as a percentage; fifty million raised at one times, exit at sixty, the preferred take fifty and a founder with twenty percent takes two million from a sale the press calls a six-fold win; not the round price, which set her percentage truly, but a floor under each round that becomes the entire payout when the exit lands near the raise, and the tell is the conversion price, above which the cap table becomes honest again.
items.why: Waterfall arithmetic is right (fifty of preference on a sixty exit leaves ten, a fifth of which is two), but 'a sale the press calls a six-fold win' is supported by nothing in the case; sixty is not six times any number given. Replace with the number the press would actually print.
items.repair: Stack that eats the common: each round's preferred takes its money back before common sees anything, so the founder's percentage is a share of the exit only above the price at which conversion beats preference, and below it a good price pays the common almost nothing; agreed round by round as 'one times non-participating, standard', understood by every investor as the whole point and read by the founder as a percentage; fifty million raised at one times, exit at sixty, the preferred take fifty and a founder with twenty percent takes two million from a sale the press reports at sixty million; not the round price, which set her percentage truly, but a floor under each round that becomes the entire payout when the exit lands near the raise, and the tell is the conversion price, above which the cap table becomes honest again.

items.item: Secondary that grows the stack: a buyer of founder or early-holder common in a secondary demands the shares be reclassified into the latest preferred, so a preference is created on shares that carried none, the stack grows by the secondary's size, and no cash reaches the company; agreed between seller and buyer, understood by the buyer's counsel, and invisible to the employees, since nothing was issued; a founder who sells five million of common at the Series C price adds five million to the stack ahead of the shares she kept and ahead of everyone's options; not the sale itself, which moves ownership at a price, but the reclassification, which moves a claim.
items.why: Reclassifying common into the latest preferred is a charter act the company must take; it cannot be 'agreed between seller and buyer' alone. The item's own point, that the claim moves without a share being issued, survives; the moment of agreement should name the board consent that makes it happen, since that is where a founder could refuse.
items.repair: Secondary that grows the stack: a buyer of founder or early-holder common in a secondary demands the shares be reclassified into the latest preferred, so a preference is created on shares that carried none, the stack grows by the secondary's size, and no cash reaches the company; agreed between seller and buyer with a board consent the company gives to make the sale happen, understood by the buyer's counsel, and invisible to the employees, since nothing was issued; a founder who sells five million of common at the Series C price adds five million to the stack ahead of the shares she kept and ahead of everyone's options; not the sale itself, which moves ownership at a price, but the reclassification, which moves a claim.

items.item: Carve-out at the door: when the exit price sits inside the stack, the preferred agree a management carve-out, a share of proceeds paid to named, still-employed executives before the waterfall, so the same founder is paid as a manager and nothing as a shareholder, and every common holder who left gets nothing; agreed at the exit, by the board, understood by the board and by no one who has already gone; a hundred-million sale against a hundred and twenty of preference with a ten-percent carve-out pays ten million to the four managers named and zero to two hundred option holders and the departed co-founder; not the stack, which is the cause, but the exception bought from it, and it forks the founder from the people who built the thing with her.
items.why: The item's case, a hundred-million sale against a hundred and twenty of preference, is the one price at which the carve-out drains the common nothing: they get zero with or without it, and the ten million comes from the preferred's own pocket. The carve-out is a carrier against the common only in the band just under the stack's top, where it takes off the top what the common would otherwise have received. The fork (founder paid as manager, the departed paid nothing) is real and kept; the arithmetic should be run where the carrier bites.
items.repair: Carve-out at the door: when the exit price sits inside the stack, the preferred agree a management carve-out, a share of proceeds paid to named, still-employed executives before the waterfall, so the same founder is paid as a manager and nothing as a shareholder, and every common holder who left gets nothing; agreed at the exit, by the board, understood by the board and by no one who has already gone; a hundred-and-fifteen-million sale against a hundred and ten of preference would pay the common five million, and a ten-percent carve-out taken off the top pays eleven and a half million to the four managers named and zero to two hundred option holders and the departed co-founder, while deeper inside the stack the same carve-out is paid from the preferred's own money and drains the common nothing; not the stack, which is the cause, but the exception bought from it, and it forks the founder from the people who built the thing with her.

items.item: Ten votes a share: the founder's class carries ten votes, so control is conserved while economics drain, and the leak is in the sunset and the transfer clauses, since the class converts to common on sale, on death, on leaving, or on a date; agreed at incorporation or at the offering, understood by the founder as permanent and by counsel as a schedule; eight percent of the economics with fifty-five percent of the vote, until a divorce transfers a block that converts on transfer and the vote falls under half; not control as such but control on a clock the founder does not see as a clock, and the tell is that the class's conversion events are listed on a page she never turned to.
items.why: Arithmetic error. At ten votes a share, a class holding eight percent of the economics carries 0.8 over 0.8 plus 0.92, which is 46.5 percent of the vote, not fifty-five; fifty-five percent needs about eleven percent of the economics. With eleven percent, a two-point block converting on transfer leaves nine, which is 49.7 percent, so the divorce case still lands under half.
items.repair: Ten votes a share: the founder's class carries ten votes, so control is conserved while economics drain, and the leak is in the sunset and the transfer clauses, since the class converts to common on sale, on death, on leaving, or on a date; agreed at incorporation or at the offering, understood by the founder as permanent and by counsel as a schedule; eleven percent of the economics with fifty-five percent of the vote, until a divorce transfers a two-point block that converts on transfer and the vote falls under half; not control as such but control on a clock the founder does not see as a clock, and the tell is that the class's conversion events are listed on a page she never turned to.

neighbor_test.left: Cap as option: a valuation cap is a ceiling, not a price, so the SAFE converts at the lower of the cap and the discounted round price, and the holder is long an option whose value grows with the uncertainty of the next round; agreed when the founder treats the cap as the valuation she raised at, understood by the investor as a floor on his percentage; a SAFE at a ten million cap converts at ten if the A prices at twenty and at six if the A prices at six, so the 'ten million round' was a ten-or-less round; not a discount, which is a fixed ratio, but a payoff bent at the cap, and the tell is a founder quoting the cap as her last valuation.
neighbor_test.right: Ratchet after the fact: anti-dilution resets an earlier round's conversion price when a later round prices lower, so the earlier investor receives shares as if she had bought at the lower price and the common pays for them; agreed in a clause the founder skips because she does not intend a down round, understood by the investor as the term that makes a high price safe; under a full ratchet a Series A that bought a quarter at four dollars sees a B at two and doubles its share count before the B buys a share, and broad-based weighted average softens this by the B's size; observed in Square's 2015 offering, where a Series E floor of $18.56 against a nine-dollar offer issued the E about ten million extra shares, as reported; not a repricing, which the investor did not buy, but a repricing in one direction only, so the earlier money holds a put on the later price.
neighbor_test.separating_case: The author's note says these are the same put written twice, so they are the pair most likely to collapse. Both are 'convert at the lower of a fixed price and the next price', and the payer is the common in both. Case: a SAFE at a ten-million cap, an A at twenty, then a B at eight. At the A the SAFE converts at the cap, the put pays nothing, and the cap is extinguished; the SAFE holder's shares are now A preferred. At the B the A holder's anti-dilution fires and resets her price toward eight; the ex-SAFE holder is protected at the B only if the shadow series she converted into carries the A's anti-dilution clause, which is the A's term and not the cap's. So the cap is a single-shot put with a strike fixed before any price exists, exercised once at conversion and gone; the ratchet is a standing put agreed after a price exists, with its strike reset at every exercise and alive through every later round. A founder can grant the first without the second (a SAFE converting into a series with no anti-dilution) and the second without the first (a priced seed). They do not collapse.

boundary_case: A conversion discount on a note or SAFE. It is agreed at signing, everyone reads it as an accounting line, its amount waits on the next round's price, and it drains ownership beyond what the founder pictured. The type still rules it out: a discount is the round price times a coefficient, so the drain runs through the price and not around it, and whoever can compute the round price can compute the drain in the same breath. Cap as option is in on the opposite finding, since the cap is a bend in the payoff and not a coefficient on it. The ruling confirms that the type's edge is 'a route other than the price', not 'a thing a founder underestimates'. A drag-along right, tried as a second nonmember, turned out to be a member the map lacks (see best_unresolved_seed).

seriation.note: The endpoints are real and opposite for the right reasons: Pool before the price is computable to the share at signing, Veto without votes never becomes a number. The consequential adjacency, Cap as option next to Ratchet after the fact, teaches something an operator can use (defend the cap and skip anti-dilution and you have defended one side of one term). Two nits. The note places Warrant on the loan 'between the signing stage and the next-price stage', but in the itinerary it sits between Below the threshold and Interest that converts, which is the signing-to-clock boundary; fix the note, not the order. Headline bought with terms waits on the exit price and so belongs with Stack and Dip twice by the declared axis, yet it is placed after Carve-out at the door, the 'room at the exit' stage; the note licenses this as the hinge, which is an authored inversion the axis sentence does not mention and should.

edges.why: The loop is real (pool paid for inside the pre-money, emptied by small grants, refilled inside the next pre-money), but 'the founders alone paid for' and 'the founder pays for the same advisors at two rounds' both fail past the first round: at the B the refill inside the pre-money dilutes the A investors too, and the refill goes to new hires, not to the same advisors. The label should carry the loop at its true strength: whoever was there before the money buys the pool the small grants empty, every round.
edges.repair_label: If the pool is sized inside the pre-money, then the grants below the threshold are drawn from shares the pre-money holders paid for, and the next lead sizes the refill inside the next pre-money, so at every round the holders who were there before the money buy the pool that the small grants emptied; the loop closes at every term sheet that says 'pre-money includes the pool'.

edges.why: Checked the strong claim that the ratcheted preferred is diluted by neither the ratchet nor the refresh. Under a full ratchet priced off the post-pool fully diluted price it holds exactly: the A's shares become A dollars over the B price per share, the B price per share is the pre-money over pre-money shares including the new pool, so the A's fraction of the pre-money is pinned at A dollars over pre-money whatever the pool size. Under weighted average it holds only in part. The label's antecedent, 'a down round triggers the ratchet', is generic; acceptable, since the item names both forms.

edges.from_handle: Reset with the trigger in the other hand
edges.why: The same-hand coupling is real: one removal decision retires the unvested shares and starts the ninety days on the vested options. But 'what falls from both lands pro rata on the hand that made it' is true only of the retired shares; lapsed options return to the pool the board regrants. The edge should show the two destinations, since that difference is what the pair teaches.
edges.repair_label: If the reset puts a founder's shares on a clock held by a board the investor can move, then her removal retires the unvested shares and starts the ninety days on her vested options, so both carriers fire from one decision: the retired shares lift every remaining holder pro rata, the hand that made the decision among them, and the lapsed options refill a pool the same board grants.

modality_problems: Ten votes a share: eight percent of the economics at ten votes a share is 46.5 percent of the vote, not fifty-five; the case needs about eleven percent (repaired).
Ninety-day guillotine and the Reset → Ninety-day edge: lapsed options return to the pool, not pro rata to remaining holders; the pro rata claim was carried over from the reset by analogy (repaired).

Warrant on the loan: 'never entered on the cap table because the warrants are worth nothing the day they are struck' is a false mechanism; an at-the-money warrant has option value and fully diluted tables commonly carry warrants; what hides it is the document (repaired).
Stack that eats the common: 'six-fold win' is supported by no number in the case (repaired).

Carve-out at the door: the illustrative price, a hundred against a hundred and twenty of preference, is one at which the carve-out drains the common nothing; the carrier bites only in the band just under the stack's top (repaired).
Reset with the trigger in the other hand: the discriminator's 'same hand' promotes 'a board the investor sits on' to the investor holding the trigger (repaired to its true strength).
Secondary that grows the stack: reclassification needs the company's consent, not only the seller's and buyer's (repaired).
Pool → Below the threshold edge: 'founders alone' and 'same advisors at two rounds' fail past the first round (repaired).

Form inference names a loop Pool → Below the threshold → Pool, but only the forward edge exists; the return is carried by the label's text ('the loop closes at every term sheet'), not by an edge. With seven edges already at the ceiling this is tolerable, but the form_inference text should say the return leg is the label's claim.
Seriation note misplaces Warrant on the loan's boundary (signing-to-clock, not signing-to-next-price) and does not license the Headline bought with terms inversion the note treats as the hinge.

Dividend nobody pays presents a cumulative dividend as standard; in venture preferred it is the less common option (NVCA offers both), more usual in growth and private equity paper. Acceptable under the boundary claim that jurisdiction and negotiation change several carriers; no repair.
duplication: none. Nearest admitted items are clean-exits' Fade by formula (dilution on a schedule the holder triggers by not paying), what-a-price-does' Price for the stranger's eyes, runway-illusions' Reach the cliff, and who-can-be-bound's Tap; all four exist as cited and the boundary claim says what each of the map's adjacent items adds. The inline cross-reference inside Headline bought with terms follows the convention already used in admitted maps.
best_unresolved_seed: Carriers that drain the preferred, which the map's conservation law predicts and its founder-facing itinerary never reaches. Pay-to-play is the sharpest: a preferred holder who does not take her pro rata of a down round is converted to common, losing her preference and her anti-dilution by a route other than price, agreed in the charter, understood by the lead who insisted on it, and firing at the next round's price; it is the founder's side of the ratchet and the only immunity-stripping term on any standard sheet. Drag-along is the second: a thing a minority may not refuse, the mirror of Veto without votes' list of things a majority may not do, and it drains control from whichever class lacks the threshold, sometimes the preferred. Both would extend the itinerary's control end and test whether the map's type really admits any drained party or only the common.
independent_review_line: Fable critic: admitted after repairing seven items and two edge labels, chiefly one wrong vote-share number, a pro rata claim that belonged to the reset and not the guillotine, and a false mechanism for the warrant's invisibility; the Cap as option and Ratchet after the fact pair survived a collapse attempt.
